title: The Two-Column Worry Sort: A Five-Minute Mental Declutter
markdown:
# The Two-Column Worry Sort: A Five-Minute Mental Declutter

## Why Most Worrying Goes Nowhere

Most worry is not actually problem-solving. It is the same loop playing on repeat: the upcoming conversation, the bill that might bounce, the thing you said that might have landed wrong. The mind treats all of this as one undifferentiated mass of concern, and because it feels urgent, it feels important. But urgency and importance are not the same thing, and a lot of what keeps circling in your head is simply noise dressed up as a task.

The practice below gives that noise a place to go. It takes five minutes, needs nothing but paper and a pen, and works by forcing a single distinction: what can you actually act on, and what can you only accept. Separating those two categories does more to quiet a busy mind than almost any amount of trying to "stop thinking about it."

## The Exercise: Two Columns, One Page

Take a sheet of paper and draw a line down the middle. Label the left column "Mine to act on" and the right column "Not mine to control." Set a timer for five minutes.

Now write down whatever is circling in your mind right now, one item at a time, and place each one in whichever column it belongs to. Do not edit yourself and do not try to solve anything yet. The only job in this step is sorting.

A few guiding questions help when an item feels ambiguous:

- Is there a concrete next action I could take today or tomorrow? If yes, left column.
- Does this depend entirely on another person's choice, a past event, or something outside my schedule? If yes, right column.
- Am I worrying about how something will turn out, rather than what I will do about it? That almost always belongs on the right.

Many people find that a worry they assumed was in the left column — something they thought they needed to "figure out" — actually belongs on the right, because what they are really anxious about is an outcome, not a task. Seeing that in writing is often more convincing than any amount of telling yourself to let it go.

### Example

Suppose your mind has been circling around a performance review next week, a friend who hasn't replied to a message in four days, and a repair bill you're waiting to hear back on.

- Performance review: left column, because you can prepare notes on your recent work and think through two questions you want to ask.
- Friend not replying: right column. You cannot control their timeline or their reasons, only your own reaction to the silence.
- Repair bill: split it. "Call the shop to ask for a status update" goes left. "Worrying about the final cost before you know it" goes right.

Notice that the repair bill shows how one worry can produce both an action and a non-action. That is normal. The point of the exercise is not to make every worry resolve cleanly, but to extract the sliver of it that is actually yours to do something about.

## What to Do With Each Column

Once the five minutes are up, look at the right column first. For each item there, say to yourself, out loud if you can, "This is not mine to control today." You are not pretending not to care. You are naming, plainly, that no amount of further thinking will change the outcome. Some people find it useful to physically fold that half of the page over, so it is out of view while they work on the left side.

Then take the left column and pick exactly one item. Not three, not all of them — one. Write underneath it the smallest possible next step, something that takes less than fifteen minutes. For the performance review example, that might be "write down two accomplishments from this month" rather than "prepare for the review," which is too large and vague to start.

Do that one small step before you do anything else today, if possible. The rest of the left column can wait for tomorrow's list. What matters is that you have converted at least one circling worry into a finished action, which tells your mind that the loop has somewhere to land.

This exercise does not make the right-column items disappear. The friend may still not reply for another week. The bill may still come back higher than you hoped. What changes is your relationship to the thinking itself: you stop mentally re-litigating the things you cannot touch, because you have already written down, in your own hand, that they do not belong to you right now.

Keep the page. If the same worry shows up again tomorrow night, sort it again. Most people find that after two or three rounds, items either move permanently into the right column, where they settle, or they resolve themselves through the small actions accumulating in the left one. Either way, the page is doing the sorting that your mind, left alone at midnight, tends to do badly.
